findings.summary: The reference-grey mark colour is reused for the value annotations of the nine non-selected rows, so the numbers a reader scans to compare variants render in a colour that measures 3.0:1 against white on the rendered PNG — below the 4.5:1 bar for 14 pt regular text, and lighter still when the 1399 px image is scaled into the evidence page's column. The row labels and the selected row's blue annotations both clear the bar, so only the comparison population reads faintly; on a projector or a discounted display those nine values are the first thing to fade.

This is the evidence fragment's decision graphic, and the left panel carries no mark for the bar the decision turns on. The plan sets at most four wrong in forty, which on this fixed screening twenty is two, and the figure shows two rows at one, eight rows at three or more and none at two. Without a threshold mark a reader cannot see from the picture that only those two rows clear the bar, nor that the selected combination's margin over the baseline (one against eleven) is far larger than its margin over the grounding-removal ablation, which scores the same one and so meets the bar on this screen as well.

Rows follow the experiment's own order — baseline, the five single changes, the two combinations, then the ablation — rather than the measured wrong count, so the two rows that meet the plan's bar sit at the bottom of the list and the baseline sits at the top. Every value is labelled directly, so each row is readable on its own; the cost is that the ranking has to be assembled by scanning all ten numbers rather than seen.

findings_note: All three findings are non-blocking: none stops a reader reading the figure. Judged from the rendered PNG attached to this review and from 200 % crops of its label column, left axis and right edge; no SVG was opened.
